mcqs.q: Attrition is best defined as the loss of tooth structure due to:
opts: Mechanical wear from an external agent
mcqs.explain: Attrition is physiological or pathological wear from tooth-to-tooth contact, with NO external agent involved.

mcqs.q: The single most important pathological cause of accelerated attrition is:
mcqs.explain: Bruxism (grinding/clenching) is the key pathological cause; brushing causes abrasion and acids cause erosion.

mcqs.q: Long-standing generalised attrition MOST characteristically reduces the:
mcqs.explain: Loss of crown height in attrition reduces the vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO).

mcqs.q: Identify the lesion shown.
mcqs.explain: Flattened incisal edges with shiny wear facets and exposed dentin are typical of attrition.

mcqs.q: In severe, untreated attrition the MOST serious dental consequence is:
mcqs.explain: As wear approaches the pulp, severe cases develop pulpal involvement and risk of tooth fracture.

mcqs.q: Which appliance is the cornerstone of managing attrition caused by bruxism?
mcqs.explain: Occlusal splints/night guards protect the teeth from parafunctional grinding forces.

mcqs.q: Abrasion differs from attrition because abrasion is produced by:
mcqs.explain: Abrasion is mechanical wear from an EXTERNAL agent (e.g. brushing), not tooth-to-tooth contact.

mcqs.q: The classic clinical appearance of advanced abrasion is a:
mcqs.explain: Horizontal brushing produces shallow cervical notches that progress to deep V/wedge-shaped defects near the CEJ.

mcqs.q: Identify the lesion shown.
mcqs.explain: A wedge-shaped cervical notch at the CEJ from horizontal/hard brushing is classic abrasion.

mcqs.q: Cervical abrasion is MOST commonly seen on the:
opts: Buccal surfaces of canines and premolars
mcqs.explain: The buccal/cervical region of canines and premolars is most frequently affected.

mcqs.q: Which habit is the MOST likely cause of cervical abrasion?
opts: Horizontal scrubbing with a hard brush
mcqs.explain: Improper horizontal brushing with a hard brush and abrasive paste is the classic cause.

mcqs.q: The recommended restorative materials for an abrasion cavity are:
mcqs.explain: Glass-ionomer cement and composite are used to restore abrasion (cervical) lesions.

mcqs.q: Erosion is caused by:
mcqs.explain: Erosion = chemical dissolution by acids of NON-bacterial origin, without mechanical force.

mcqs.q: Which is an INTRINSIC source of acid in dental erosion?
mcqs.explain: Intrinsic acid comes from GERD and chronic vomiting; the others are extrinsic/environmental.

mcqs.q: Intrinsic erosion (reflux/vomiting) characteristically affects the:
mcqs.explain: Regurgitated acid pools palatally on the upper teeth, so palatal maxillary surfaces are typically eroded.

mcqs.q: Identify the lesion shown.
mcqs.explain: Smooth, rounded cupping of the occlusal surface with loss of detail is typical of erosion.

mcqs.q: Which surface feature MOST suggests erosion rather than attrition?
opts: Smooth, shiny surface with loss of detail
mcqs.explain: Eroded enamel is smooth and shiny with loss of anatomical detail (cupping), unlike sharp attritional facets.

mcqs.q: Which is an EXTRINSIC dietary cause of erosion?
mcqs.explain: Citrus fruits, carbonated and sports drinks are extrinsic dietary acids (tablets are medicinal, fumes environmental).

mcqs.q: Beyond dietary advice, a key management step for intrinsic erosion is:
mcqs.explain: Intrinsic erosion needs medical referral to control GERD/vomiting, plus fluoride and remineralising agents.

mcqs.q: Internal resorption is the loss of dentin that begins:
opts: From within the pulp chamber / canal
mcqs.explain: Internal resorption arises from clastic activity of pulpal origin, eroding dentin from inside the canal.

mcqs.q: The 'pink tooth' appearance is pathognomonic of:
mcqs.explain: Vascular granulation tissue of internal resorption shows through the thinned dentin as a pink spot.

mcqs.q: Identify the condition shown.
mcqs.explain: The pink area within the crown is the classic 'pink tooth' of internal resorption.

mcqs.q: On a radiograph, internal resorption typically appears as a radiolucency that is:
opts: Irregular and shifts with beam angulation
Centred on and continuous with the canal
mcqs.explain: Internal resorption is round/oval, continuous with the pulp space and stays centred on the canal on angled films.

mcqs.q: A common initiating cause of internal resorption is:
mcqs.explain: Chronic pulpal inflammation, trauma, infection and iatrogenic heat are causes; ortho force causes EXTERNAL resorption.

mcqs.q: The definitive management of internal resorption usually involves:
mcqs.explain: Removing the inflamed pulp (endodontics) with Ca(OH)₂ medicament arrests internal resorption; MTA repairs perforation.

mcqs.q: External resorption involves the loss of:
opts: Dentin only, from within the pulp
Cementum and dentin from the external root surface
mcqs.explain: External resorption removes cementum and dentin starting at the external root surface, by clastic activity.

mcqs.q: Which factor is a recognised cause of EXTERNAL resorption?
mcqs.explain: Trauma (luxation/avulsion), excessive orthodontic force, periapical/periodontal inflammation and pressure from cysts/tumours cause external resorption.

mcqs.q: Identify the finding shown on this extracted tooth.
mcqs.explain: The irregular defect eroding the external root surface is external root resorption.

mcqs.q: On a radiograph, external resorption is distinguished because the lesion:
opts: Shifts position with change in beam angulation
mcqs.explain: Being on the surface, an external lesion moves with angulation (parallax/SLOB), unlike the canal-centred internal lesion.

mcqs.q: Both internal and external resorption are fundamentally driven by:
mcqs.explain: Resorption of dental hard tissue is mediated by clastic (odontoclast) cells in both forms.

saqs.q: Define attrition and state why it lowers the vertical dimension of occlusion.
saqs.a: Tooth-to-tooth wear without external agents. It flattens cusps/incisal edges and reduces crown height, so the closed-mouth jaw position shortens → the VDO drops.

saqs.q: List four causes of dental erosion.
saqs.a:
1. Extrinsic — citrus, carbonated/sports drinks
2. Intrinsic — GERD / vomiting
3. Environmental — industrial fumes, chlorinated pools
4. Medications — vitamin C, aspirin

saqs.q: Compare attrition, abrasion and erosion (cause and typical lesion).
saqs.a:
TypeCauseLesion
AttritionTooth-to-toothFlat facets, ↓ crown height
AbrasionExternal mechanical (brushing)V-shaped cervical notch
ErosionAcid (non-bacterial)Smooth cupping; palatal of upper teeth

saqs.q: A 28-year-old with self-induced vomiting has smooth cupping and wear of the palatal upper anteriors. What is the lesion and the key management?
saqs.a: Intrinsic erosion. Refer to control the vomiting/GERD; fluoride & remineralisation; desensitisers; composite or veneers.

saqs.q: Distinguish internal from external root resorption.
saqs.a:
FeatureInternalExternal
OriginPulpRoot surface (cementum & dentin)
Sign'Pink tooth'Root shortening
X-rayCentred on canalShifts with angulation (parallax)

saqs.q: An asymptomatic upper incisor shows a pink spot; a periapical film shows an oval radiolucency centred on the canal. Diagnosis and management?
saqs.a: Internal resorption. Endodontic treatment with calcium hydroxide; obturate with gutta-percha; MTA for any perforation.
